analysis.one_liner: Lets banks opt out of Sarbanes-Oxley executive certifications and internal-control checks.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in March 2007, drew no cosponsors, and died when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, the investor-protection law passed after the Enron and WorldCom accounting scandals. It would have required the Securities and Exchange Commission to let banks, bank holding companies, and savings-and-loan holding companies opt out of two key requirements: the rule that a company's top executives personally certify the accuracy of its financial reports, and the rule that companies report on whether their internal controls against fraud actually work. A company could have taken this option voluntarily. The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, publicly traded banks and their holding companies would have saved the cost of preparing executive certifications and internal-control reports, and their executives would have been relieved of personal legal accountability for the accuracy of financial statements they signed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Publicly traded banks and their holding companies

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have required the SEC's rules to allow any insured depository institution, bank holding company, or savings-and-loan holding company to elect not to provide the executive certifications on quarterly and annual reports that Sarbanes-Oxley section 302 requires of public companies. [S2] [S3]

It would have likewise allowed those same institutions to opt out of the internal-control report under Sarbanes-Oxley section 404, in which management assesses whether the company's controls over financial reporting are effective. [S2] [S3]
The election was voluntary, so a bank could decide filing by filing whether to skip the certifications and internal-control report. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Investors in bank stocks would have borne the cost: they would have lost the executive certifications and internal-control disclosures that help them judge whether a bank's reported financials are trustworthy, and the public would have borne more risk that accounting problems at banks go undetected, as happened in the scandals that prompted Sarbanes-Oxley.
analysis.who_pays_short: Investors in bank stocks and the public

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden is real: preparing internal-control reports and executive certifications costs banks money and management time, and an honest supporter could argue that for banks the same firms are already examined by bank regulators, so the duplication is expense without much added protection. [S2]

The opt-out design could have backfired on the banks themselves: because the election was voluntary, investors might have treated a bank's decision to skip certification as a red flag, discounting its stock or questioning its filings, without any guarantee the savings outweighed that cost. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings to banks from skipping these reports would have come directly out of the information investors rely on to spot accounting trouble. Sarbanes-Oxley's executive certification and internal-control requirements were enacted precisely because weak internal controls let major corporate frauds go undetected, and exempting an entire regulated industry would have reopened that gap. Whatever burden the rules impose, this bill offered no replacement safeguard.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, got no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Walter B. Jones Jr. of North Carolina introduced the bill on March 15, 2007. [S1] [S5]
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, which is where the action ended. [S1] [S5]
No other member signed on as a cosponsor. [S4]
The committee never reported the bill, and no chamber voted on it before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009. [S1] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Investors in bank stocks and the public kept the full Sarbanes-Oxley protections intact. Bank holding companies, which would have gained an opt-out from executive certifications and internal-control reporting, gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Walter B. Jones Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Financial Services Committee; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Barney Frank (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or reported the bill out, so it never reached the House floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had a single sponsor with zero cosponsors, so there is no record of partisan or bipartisan support.

industries.industry: Publicly traded banks and bank holding companies
industries.note: The bill would have let these companies skip executive certifications and internal-control reporting, cutting their compliance costs. That savings came directly out of the disclosures investors use to detect accounting trouble at banks, so the industry's gain was the public's reduced protection. The bill died, so the banks gained nothing.

Firms that help companies prepare Sarbanes-Oxley internal-control reports would have lost business if banks could opt out. Their interest ran alongside investors' interest in keeping the controls in place.
